title: Exploring automatic scoring of mathematical descriptive assessment using prompt engineering with the GPT-4 model: Focused on permutations and combinations
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether GPT-4-based ChatGPT can automatically score mathematical descriptive assessment items in a way that aligns with human teachers. The authors focus on the challenge that scoring constructed-response mathematics items is time-consuming for teachers and can be difficult to make consistent, especially when problems allow multiple solution strategies.

The study uses prompt engineering to improve GPT-4’s scoring performance. The researchers designed structured prompts using techniques such as Few-Shot-CoT, Self-Consistency, and iterative prompt refinement. For one item with multiple solution strategies, they also added a classification step so GPT-4 first identified the solution type and then applied a type-specific scoring prompt. Teacher scoring was used as the comparison benchmark.

The participants were 204 first-year high school students in one high school in Suwon, South Korea, who completed three permutation-and-combination descriptive items. Two experienced teachers scored the responses and their scores were compared with GPT-4’s scores. The paper concludes that GPT-4’s scores were strongly correlated with teacher scores, and that self-consistency improved reliability. It also found that classification by solution strategy substantially improved GPT-4 performance on the item with multiple valid approaches, suggesting that prompt engineering can help GPT-4 function as a scoring aid for teachers.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical correlational study comparing GPT-4 scoring with two teachers on real student responses, but it is not an RCT and does not isolate causal effects on learning. The evidence is useful but limited to a single school, a small set of items, and grading agreement outcomes rather than student achievement gains.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a modest practical benefit for grading efficiency and scoring consistency, especially for constructed-response math items. However, it does not test student learning outcomes or show large-scale operational impact, so the observed impact is promising but still unclear/modest.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-based automatic scoring of middle/high school students' descriptive mathematics answers in permutations and combinations, using prompt engineering, few-shot CoT, self-consistency, and structured prompts to emulate teacher grading.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that GPT-4 can support teacher scoring of mathematical constructed-response items with strong teacher-model correlations, suggesting potential workload reduction in grading descriptive assessments. For items 1 and 2, teacher vs. GPT-4 scoring correlations were high (roughly r=0.80-0.91 across individual runs; mode correlations 0.872-0.905), and for item 3 correlations improved further after answer-type classification (mode correlations 0.928-0.931), indicating a practical grading-aid use case.
finding.measure: Correlation between teacher scoring and GPT-4 scoring; consistency of GPT-4 scoring across repeated runs
finding.study_size: n=197 (items 1 and 2), n=174 (item 3); correlations reported on subsets after excluding non-mode cases

finding.finding_summary: The system demonstrated strong agreement with teacher grading on permutation and combination constructed-response items, indicating that GPT-4 can accurately evaluate mathematical reasoning and symbolic expression in this content area. Correlations between teacher and GPT-4 scores were about 0.8 overall, with stronger performance on items 1 and 2 and improved alignment on item 3 when responses were first classified by solution strategy.
finding.measure: Teacher-grade vs GPT-4-grade correlation on mathematics descriptive assessment items
finding.study_size: n=197 for items 1-2; n=174 for item 3
